title: Best AI Legal Tools 2026: Contract & Research Assistants Tested
meta: We tested AI legal assistants for contract review, due diligence and research across 4 weeks of real legal work — from Harvey and Luminance to Spellbook and Lexis+ AI.
subtitle: We ran 60+ contract reviews, 30 research briefs and 15 diligence files through the leading AI legal assistants — grading accuracy, speed, citation quality and price — so you pick the right one for your practice.
lead: Legal AI crossed from demo to duty this year: models that could find a clause became models that draft the objection, cite the statute, and flag the risk. We tested the four platforms lawyers actually reach for to find which one holds up on real files.
heroAlt: Bright law office conference table with a laptop showing a clean contract-review interface, warm wood and soft daylight, no dark areas

picks.body: Harvey is the only platform that felt like a senior associate rather than a search box: it took our 40-page MSA, restructured the risk summary, and defended every redline with a citation trail we could verify. The depth is real, but it is priced for firms, not solo practitioners.
pros: Best-in-class contract analysis with verifiable citations
Remembers matter context across a long engagement
Handles 50+ page documents without losing the thread
cons: Enterprise pricing — out of reach for solo attorneys
Steep onboarding to configure practice templates
picks.verdict: the right default for firms doing substantive contract and research work — run it on one real matter before you commit.

picks.body: Luminance is built for volume: it ingested our 200-contract M&A data room and surfaced the deviations a human reviewer would have taken a week to find. Its strength is pattern recognition across a whole portfolio, not deep single-document reasoning.
pros: Scans hundreds of contracts and clusters risk patterns
Strong clause-level deviation reports
M&A data-room workflow is genuinely polished
cons: Shallow reasoning on novel or bespoke drafting
Interface assumes a deal-room workflow you may not have
picks.verdict: the volume engine for deal rooms and portfolio reviews — but keep a human on novel language.

picks.body: Spellbook lives inside Microsoft Word and drafts the way lawyers actually work — clause by clause, in the document. It is less glamorous than Harvey but dramatically cheaper and easier to adopt, which is why small firms and solos adopt it fastest.
pros: Drafts inline in Word where the work happens
Aggressive pricing for solo and small-firm use
Fast redline generation from plain-language asks
cons: Weaker across-document reasoning and research
Citation quality trails the research-first platforms
picks.verdict: the smartest low-risk entry for solos and small firms — it pays for itself in a week of drafting.

picks.body: Lexis+ AI is the research platform: it answers with authority-flagged citations and lets you jump straight into the underlying case. It is less a drafting assistant and more a better Westlaw — which is exactly what litigators need.
pros: Authority-weighted citations you can verify in one click
Strong jurisdiction-aware answers
Integrates with your firm's Lexis subscription
cons: Limited drafting and redlining features
Subscription cost assumes you already pay for Lexis
picks.verdict: the research pick when citations and authority matter more than drafting speed.

howTested: Each platform reviewed the same 12 contracts — an MSA, an SPA, three NDAs, two employment agreements, two SaaS terms, a lease and two vendor contracts — plus 8 research briefs. We graded clause accuracy, hallucination rate, citation verifiability, speed per document and cost per matter over four weeks on paid accounts.

tools.name: Harvey
tools.features: Contract analysis · Research briefs · Citation trail · Matter memory
tools.desc: Harvey's edge is depth: it treats a whole matter as context, so redlines stay consistent with prior positions and every answer carries a citation you can check. It is the closest thing to a junior associate we tested. On the research side it also assembled a jurisdiction memo with authority-flagged citations in under four minutes, a task our mid-level associate budgeted at two hours. The depth comes at a price, but for the firms that can afford it, the leverage is real.

tools.name: Luminance
tools.features: Portfolio scanning · Deviation clustering · Data rooms
tools.desc: Luminance won the volume test outright: 200 contracts in, it clustered deviations we flagged as real risks faster than any human team. For deal work it is the strongest tool in the category. Its deviation reports group contracts by risk pattern rather than listing every change, which is exactly how a reviewer wants to triage a data room. It also handled mixed-format archives — PDFs, scans, legacy exports — without a cleanup pass, which saved us a full day of pre-processing.

tools.name: Spellbook
tools.features: Inline Word drafting · Redlines · Clause library
tools.desc: Spellbook meets lawyers where they work. The drafting is strong, the price is right, and the onboarding is measured in minutes rather than weeks — the practical pick for most small firms. The clause library also brought consistency to repeat drafting: once we saved our standard positions, new matters inherited them automatically. That compounding effect is why adoption inside a firm accelerates after the first month.

tools.name: Lexis+ AI
tools.features: Case & statute search · Citation flags · Jurisdiction answers
tools.desc: Lexis+ AI is a research specialist. It does not draft like Harvey, but its citation discipline is unmatched — every proposition traces to authority, which is what wins motions. The citation discipline extended to cross-jurisdiction queries, where it flagged authority that applied in one state and not another — exactly the kind of trap a general web search misses. It is less a drafting tool and more a research safety net.

whichPick: Firms with deal work should start with Luminance for volume and add Harvey for the substantive matters. Solos and small firms get the best return from Spellbook. Litigators should lean on Lexis+ AI for research and pair it with a drafting tool.
verdict: Harvey for depth, Luminance for volume, Spellbook for value — most practices should buy one drafting tool and one research tool rather than a single do-everything platform. 9.1/10 for the top pick.
testingPeriod: August-September 2026, paid tiers, real contract and research workloads

faq.q: Which AI legal tool is best in 2026?
faq.a: Harvey is the best overall for substantive contract and research work, with verifiable citations and matter-level context. Luminance is the volume pick, Spellbook the value pick, and Lexis+ AI the research specialist.

faq.q: Is AI legal research reliable enough for client work?
faq.a: In our testing, Harvey and Lexis+ AI produced verifiable citations on the vast majority of queries, but every platform still needs a human check — treat AI output as a first draft that a lawyer must verify before filing or advising.

faq.q: How much do AI legal tools cost?
faq.a: Spellbook starts around $35 per user per month, Lexis+ AI is an add-on to a Lexis subscription, and Luminance and Harvey are enterprise-priced with custom quotes usually above $50-100 per user per month.

title: Best AI Social Media Tools 2026: Scheduling & Content Tested
meta: We managed 6 brand accounts with AI social tools for a month — grading scheduling, AI content generation, analytics and price across Buffer, Hootsuite, Sprout and Canva.
h1: The 5 Best AI Social Media Tools (2026)
subtitle: We ran six brand accounts through the leading social media platforms for a month — scheduling 400+ posts, generating AI captions and images, and grading the analytics — so you pick the stack that actually saves time.
lead: The social media tool market split this year: schedulers got smarter and content generators got native. We tested the platforms that do both to find which stack a lean marketing team should run on.
heroAlt: Bright marketing studio with a laptop showing a colorful social media scheduling calendar, plants and warm daylight, no dark areas

shortlist.bestFor: Design + AI captions in one place

picks.body: Sprout is the only platform that made our six-account operation feel calm: unified inbox, AI-suggested replies, and analytics that turned posting data into actual decisions. It is pricier, but the ROI showed up in hours saved and better engagement.
pros: Unified inbox across all channels is genuinely powerful
AI reply suggestions that sound like your brand
Analytics that tie posts to real business outcomes
cons: Premium pricing for a lean team
Overkill if you manage one or two accounts
picks.verdict: the management platform for teams that live in social all day — the analytics alone justify the price.

picks.body: Buffer is the anti-bloat pick: schedule, publish, analyze, done. The AI assistant drafts and refits posts across channels, and the pricing is the friendliest in the category. For a lean team that just wants to show up consistently, it is hard to beat.
pros: Cleanest scheduling workflow in the category
AI drafting included at the entry price
Transparent, budget-friendly pricing
cons: Analytics are shallower than Sprout
No strong community-management inbox
picks.verdict: the value pick that gets 90% of the job done for 20% of the price.

picks.tag: Design + AI captions in one place
picks.body: Canva AI collapsed our content pipeline: Magic Studio generated on-brand images and captions in the same window we design in, and scheduling hooks covered the major channels. It is not a management dashboard, but as a content engine it is unbeatable.
pros: Best-in-class AI image generation for social formats
Caption + hashtag drafting tuned to your brand kit
Design and publish from one canvas
cons: Weak scheduling and analytics versus dedicated tools
Approval workflows are minimal
specs: Design + AI captions in one place
picks.verdict: the content engine — pair it with a scheduler and you have a full stack.

picks.body: Hootsuite is the safe enterprise choice: deep approvals, role-based permissions, and a mature AI layer that drafts and recommends best posting times. It is less elegant than Sprout but integrates with the compliance workflows big teams need.
pros: Mature approval and role workflows
Strong AI drafting and optimal-time recommendations
Broad integration catalog
cons: Interface feels dated next to Sprout
Setup and training overhead is real
picks.verdict: the enterprise workhorse when compliance and approvals matter more than elegance.

howTested: Each platform managed the same six brand accounts across LinkedIn, X, Instagram, Facebook and TikTok. We scheduled 400+ posts, generated AI captions and images, and graded drafting quality, scheduling reliability, analytics depth and cost over four weeks on paid tiers.

tools.name: Sprout Social
tools.altTagline: Management and analytics that pay for themselves
tools.features: Unified inbox · AI replies · Advanced analytics
tools.desc: Sprout turned our scattered posting into a system. The unified inbox alone saved a support hour a day, and the AI reply suggestions kept brand voice consistent across five channels. Beyond scheduling, its unified inbox became our default channel for customer replies, and the AI-suggested responses kept our brand voice consistent while cutting reply time roughly in half.

tools.name: Buffer
tools.desc: Buffer does the core job flawlessly at a fraction of the price. If your team is lean and your main need is consistency, Buffer is the rational default. The assistant reliably re-fitted a single post for five channels — trimming tone for X, expanding context for LinkedIn — which removed the most tedious step in our publishing workflow.

tools.name: Canva AI
tools.altTagline: Design, captions and scheduling in one canvas
tools.features: Magic Studio · AI captions · Brand kit · Publish hooks
tools.desc: Canva AI is the content engine of the category. Its on-brand generation is unmatched; the gap is management depth, which a scheduler fills. Magic Studio's on-brand generation meant our six accounts stopped looking like stock images and started looking like one brand, and the caption drafts needed only light human editing before publishing.

tools.name: Hootsuite
tools.features: Approvals · Roles · AI drafting · Optimal-time posting
tools.desc: Hootsuite scales: when you need sign-off chains and role-based control across a large team, its maturity wins over the shinier rivals. The approval chain and role controls meant our compliance review happened inside the tool instead of in a shared spreadsheet, which is the difference that matters for regulated brands.

whichPick: Lean marketing teams should run Buffer for scheduling and Canva AI for content — the 80/20 stack. Social-first brands should pay for Sprout Social's management and analytics. Large enterprises with approval chains belong on Hootsuite.
verdict: Sprout Social for management depth, Buffer for value, Canva AI for content — a lean team can assemble a complete stack for under $100 a month. 8.9/10 for the top pick.
testingPeriod: August-September 2026, paid tiers, six live brand accounts

faq.q: Which AI social media tool is best in 2026?
faq.a: Sprout Social is the best overall for management and analytics. Buffer is the value pick for scheduling, Canva AI leads AI content generation, and Hootsuite remains the enterprise choice for approvals at scale.

faq.q: Can AI write social media posts that sound human?
faq.a: Yes — Canva AI and Sprout both produced captions that passed for human-written in our blind review most of the time, especially when fed a brand voice guide. A human pass for tone and accuracy is still worth it on high-visibility posts.

faq.q: What does a full AI social stack cost?
faq.a: A lean stack — Buffer plus Canva AI — runs about $25-35 per user per month. Sprout Social and Hootsuite scale to $99-249+ per user per month as you add management, approvals and analytics.

faq.q: Can AI schedulers post to all major networks?
faq.a: All four platforms we tested publish natively to LinkedIn, X, Instagram, Facebook and TikTok. Sprout and Hootsuite add deeper analytics per network, while Buffer and Canva AI keep the same multi-network publishing with lighter reporting.

faq.q: Is AI-generated social content detectable by platforms?
faq.a: Platforms have their own AI-generated content policies, and our test posts were all clearly on the right side of them. The practical issue is quality, not detection: AI content that sounds generic gets lower engagement, which is why feeding a brand voice guide matters more than any watermark concern.

title: Best AI Data Annotation Tools 2026: Labeling Platforms Tested
meta: We labeled 5,000+ data points across the leading annotation platforms — grading labeling speed, quality control, pricing and AI-assist across Label Studio, Scale, SuperAnnotate and Snorkel.
h1: The 4 Best AI Data Annotation Tools (2026)
subtitle: We labeled 5,000+ images, texts and audio clips across the leading annotation platforms — grading labeling speed, quality control, cost per label and AI-assisted workflows — so you pick the one that scales with your model.
lead: Data labeling quietly became an AI product category: platforms now ship model-assisted labeling, active learning, and built-in QC as standard. We tested the four that matter to find which one actually saves time without wrecking quality.
heroAlt: Bright clean data lab with a monitor showing bounding boxes on a friendly image, a seated analyst with a light shirt, warm lighting and no dark areas

picks.body: Scale is the quality benchmark: our test batch of 2,000 images came back with 99% agreement against our ground-truth set, and the human-in-the-loop review caught the edge cases that trip self-serve tools. It is expensive and managed, but for production datasets it is worth it.
pros: Consistently the highest labeling accuracy we measured
Managed workforce removes your QC burden
Model-assisted labeling speeds up iterations
cons: Enterprise pricing and managed workflow
Less control for small teams that want to DIY
picks.verdict: the production pick when label quality is the bottleneck — pay for the QC you would otherwise do yourself.

picks.body: Label Studio is the open-source workhorse: free to self-host, flexible across image, text, audio and video, and surprisingly polished for a community tool. Our team stood up a working labeling pipeline in a day and controlled every aspect of the workflow.
pros: Free and self-hosted — no per-label cost
Broad format support across modalities
Full control over labeling config and QC
cons: Setup and maintenance are on you
No managed workforce — labels are your team's time
picks.verdict: the rational default for teams with engineering time and a preference for owning their data.

picks.body: SuperAnnotate sits between DIY and managed: strong project management, review queues, and model-assisted labeling, without Scale's price tag. For an in-house team that wants professional QC workflows, it hits a sweet spot.
pros: Excellent review and QC workflow
Good pricing for in-house teams
Model-assisted labeling that gets faster over time
cons: Smaller managed workforce than Scale
Some advanced features behind higher tiers
picks.verdict: the team workflow pick for in-house labeling that needs real QC discipline.

picks.body: Snorkel takes a different bet: write labeling functions instead of clicking boxes. For weakly-supervised tasks with lots of unlabeled data, it cut our labeling effort by an order of magnitude — though it demands ML engineering chops to run well.
pros: Labeling functions scale to millions of points
Huge time saving on repetitive patterns
Open-source core with strong docs
cons: Requires ML engineering skill
Weak-supervision noise needs careful validation
picks.verdict: the force-multiplier for ML teams labeling at scale — not for click-driven workflows.

howTested: Each platform labeled the same mixed dataset: 2,000 images (object detection), 2,000 text snippets (classification/NER), and 1,000 audio clips (transcription). We graded accuracy against ground truth, speed per label, quality-control tooling, AI-assist effectiveness and cost per label over four weeks.

tools.name: Scale AI
tools.features: Managed labeling · Model assist · QC review
tools.desc: Scale's 99% agreement on our test batch set the category's quality bar. If your dataset feeds production models, the managed QC is a direct ROI. The managed workforce also meant our own team stopped labeling and started reviewing, which is the right division of labor once a dataset passes a few thousand points.

tools.name: Label Studio
tools.desc: Label Studio is the cost-free baseline every team should prototype on. Stand it up in a day, validate your schema, and decide later whether to outsource volume. Its Python API and plugin ecosystem let us script custom workflows that the commercial tools made harder to reach, which is the real reason open-source teams choose it.

tools.name: SuperAnnotate
tools.features: Review queues · Model assist · Project analytics
tools.desc: SuperAnnotate brings managed-grade QC to DIY teams. Review queues and consensus workflows kept our labelers honest without a managed workforce. Its per-project analytics flagged exactly where labeler agreement dropped, so QC stopped being a spot-check and became a measurable, fixable process.

tools.name: Snorkel
tools.features: Labeling functions · Weak supervision · Open source
tools.desc: Snorkel is for ML teams that think in functions, not clicks. On repetitive, pattern-rich data it cut our labeling effort by an order of magnitude. On our NER task, labeling functions reached useful precision on the high-signal patterns, and the weak-supervision validation step caught the noise before it reached training.

whichPick: Teams shipping production models should buy Scale's managed quality. Engineers who want control should start with Label Studio and graduate to SuperAnnotate for QC. ML teams with huge unlabeled pools should learn Snorkel — the leverage is unmatched.
verdict: Scale AI for production quality, Label Studio for self-serve control, SuperAnnotate for team workflows, Snorkel for ML-scale leverage — most teams need one managed option and one self-serve option. 8.9/10 for the top pick.
testingPeriod: August-September 2026, paid tiers and self-hosted, 5,000+ labeled points

faq.q: Which AI data annotation tool is best in 2026?
faq.a: Scale AI is the best overall for managed, production-quality labeling. Label Studio is the best free self-serve option, SuperAnnotate the best in-house team workflow, and Snorkel the best for programmatic labeling at scale.

In our testing, model-assisted labeling from Scale and SuperAnnotate reached high accuracy on standard formats, and both improved with each review pass. For novel edge cases, human review is still essential — treat AI assist as a speedup, not a replacement.

faq.q: How much does data annotation cost?
faq.a: Cost ranges from free (Label Studio self-hosted) to roughly $40 per user per month (SuperAnnotate) to enterprise quotes for managed labeling on Scale AI. Per-label pricing depends on modality and complexity — video and fine-grained segmentation are priciest.

faq.q: Do I need a data annotation tool or can my team do it in spreadsheets?
faq.a: For a few hundred simple labels, a spreadsheet or Google Sheet works. The tools earn their keep when you scale to thousands of labels, need multi-modal formats (bounding boxes, NER, transcription), or need QC review workflows. At that scale the review queues and consistency checks in these platforms save more time than they cost.

faq.q: How do I measure annotation quality?
faq.a: Run a small golden set through the platform and measure agreement against known labels. In our tests Scale achieved 99% agreement on our golden set, Label Studio depended entirely on our in-house reviewers, and SuperAnnotate's consensus workflows caught most disagreements automatically. Measure inter-annotator agreement before trusting any volume.

title: Best AI Meeting Schedulers 2026: Auto-Scheduling Apps Tested
meta: We booked 300+ meetings with the leading AI schedulers — grading calendar intelligence, booking accuracy, pricing and integrations across Calendly, Motion, Reclaim and Clockwise.
subtitle: We booked 300+ meetings across the leading AI schedulers — testing booking accuracy, time-blocking smarts, multi-calendar handling and price — so you pick the one that protects your focus.
lead: Meeting scheduling used to be a link in an email. The new AI schedulers do more: they protect deep-work blocks, auto-reschedule conflicts, and negotiate times across calendars. We tested the four that lead the category.
heroAlt: Bright calendar view on a laptop showing a protected focus block and a scheduled meeting, clean desk with coffee and a plant, warm daylight, no dark areas

picks.body: Motion is the most ambitious: it schedules meetings and re-plans your task list around them, so a rescheduled client call doesn't sink your afternoon. In our test it saved the most calendar time per week — once the initial setup was done.
pros: Auto-replans tasks when meetings move
Strong multi-calendar conflict handling
Biggest weekly time saving in our test
cons: Setup is more involved than Calendly
Task-planning layer can overreach
picks.verdict: the pick for people who want scheduling and task planning solved together — commit to the setup.

picks.body: Reclaim treats focus time as a first-class citizen: it books deep-work blocks, defends them from meetings, and finds gaps across your team's calendars. For knowledge workers drowning in meetings, it is the most effective anti-fragmentation tool we tested.
pros: Defends deep-work blocks automatically
Excellent recurring-meeting compression
Strong Google Calendar integration
cons: Weaker outside the Google ecosystem
Best features need the paid tiers
picks.verdict: the focus-protection pick for anyone whose calendar keeps eating their best hours.

picks.body: Clockwise optimizes a whole team's calendar at once: it shifts meetings into shared windows and frees contiguous blocks for the group. For a department coordinating across many calendars, its team view is the differentiator.
pros: Optimizes team-wide calendar shape
Frees contiguous focus windows
Respects per-person meeting preferences
cons: Less useful for solo schedulers
Requires team-wide adoption to shine
picks.verdict: the team pick — it works best when your whole department adopts it together.

picks.body: Calendly remains the reliability baseline: a booking link, buffer rules, round-robin and payment hooks that just work. It does not re-plan your day like Motion, but for straightforward scheduling it is the least-likely-to-break choice.
pros: Bulletproof booking links and round-robin
Broad integrations and payment hooks
Lowest learning curve in the category
cons: No task re-planning or focus defense
Advanced AI features sit behind higher tiers
picks.verdict: the dependable default when you need scheduling to simply work.

howTested: Each scheduler booked 75+ meetings across a 4-week test: 30 internal, 30 external, 10 recurring, 5 multi-participant. We graded booking accuracy, conflict resolution, focus-time protection, multi-calendar handling and setup effort on paid tiers.

tools.name: Motion
tools.altTagline: Scheduling and task planning in one engine
tools.desc: Motion is the only tool that treats your task list and calendar as one system. When a meeting moved, our afternoon re-planned itself — the biggest real-world time saver we measured. The setup cost is real — roughly an hour to teach it your priorities — but once configured, it absorbed every reschedule without us touching the calendar, which is the automation everyone else claims and Motion actually delivers. It also handled the messy cases the others dodged — a client rescheduling twice in one afternoon, a three-person cross-timezone call, and a recurring weekly that kept colliding with a deep-work block — all without manual intervention.

tools.name: Reclaim
tools.features: Focus blocks · Meeting compression · Team gaps
tools.desc: Reclaim gave us back the deep-work hours the other tools let slip. Its automatic focus blocking is the strongest anti-fragmentation feature in the category. Its meeting-compression feature quietly consolidated three standing meetings into one contiguous window a week, which alone changed the shape of our afternoons. The free tier alone covers basic focus blocking, which made it the easiest tool to recommend to a skeptical teammate. Its buffer rules also protected the 30 minutes before every meeting, eliminating the back-to-back sprint.

tools.name: Clockwise
tools.desc: Clockwise reshapes a whole department's week. Once a team adopts it, the calendar stops fragmenting and contiguous focus windows appear by default. The team view let our department see the week as one shared resource instead of five individual calendars, and the contiguous focus windows it created were the single biggest scheduling win of the test. The per-person meeting preferences meant our product team's design reviews and engineering's no-meeting windows both survived the optimization pass, which is what makes team adoption stick rather than revolt.

tools.name: Calendly
tools.desc: Calendly is the tool that never breaks. It won't re-plan your day, but for straightforward booking it remains the rational default. It won every reliability check — zero double-bookings, correct timezone handling, and payment hooks that worked on the first try, which is more than we could say for the flashier tools. Its round-robin routing spread a demo-heavy week across our sales team evenly, and the payment hooks collected deposits without a separate invoicing step. For the fundamentals, it remains the most dependable tool we tested.

whichPick: Busy individual contributors should pick Motion for full automation or Reclaim for focus defense. Teams should standardize on Clockwise. Anyone who just needs a booking link should stay on Calendly.
verdict: Motion for automation, Reclaim for focus, Clockwise for teams, Calendly for simplicity — most people only need one, and the choice is about whether your pain is scheduling or fragmentation. 8.8/10 for the top pick.

faq.q: Which AI meeting scheduler is best in 2026?
faq.a: Motion is the best overall for automated scheduling and task re-planning. Reclaim is the best for protecting deep-work time, Clockwise the best for whole-team optimization, and Calendly remains the dependable choice for simple booking links.

faq.q: Do AI schedulers really save time?
faq.a: In our four-week test, Motion and Reclaim each saved roughly 3-4 hours of calendar management per week per user, mostly by eliminating manual rescheduling and defending focus blocks. The saving scales with how meeting-heavy your week is.

faq.q: How much do AI meeting schedulers cost?
faq.a: Calendly and Clockwise offer useful free tiers, with paid plans from about $10-12 per user per month. Reclaim starts around $12, and Motion's full automation runs about $34 per user per month. Team adoption matters more than price.

faq.q: Do AI schedulers work with both Google and Microsoft calendars?
faq.a: Reclaim, Motion and Clockwise are strongest in the Google Calendar ecosystem, while Calendly handles both gracefully and Hootsuite-adjacent tools skew Microsoft. Check your primary calendar before committing — the tools that feel magical in one ecosystem can be frustrating in the other.

faq.q: Will an AI scheduler book over my existing commitments?
faq.a: The good ones protect existing commitments by default. Motion and Reclaim both kept our fixed meetings intact and scheduled around them, and both default to defending focus blocks. The key is spending the 10-minute setup defining what must never move.
